items.topic: What happens after you submit your application
items.hook: Here is what actually happens after you hit submit.
items.visual_concept: A sequence of matte planes receding in depth, each catching progressively cooler light
key_points: You receive a filing receipt with a serial number confirming the date
The application waits in a queue for assignment to an examining attorney
The examining attorney reviews it against the register and the rules
If it clears, it publishes for opposition before registration issues

stages.label: Filing receipt
stages.detail: A serial number confirms your filing date

stages.label: Examination
stages.detail: An examining attorney reviews the application

stages.label: Office Action
stages.detail: Issued only if something needs addressing

stages.label: Publication
stages.detail: Others get a window to oppose

items.caption_body:
Submitting is the visible part. Almost everything that decides the outcome happens afterwards, quietly.

You get a filing receipt with a serial number. That fixes your date.

Then the application waits to be assigned to an examining attorney, who reviews it against the register and against the rules for registrability.

If something needs addressing, an Office Action is issued and you respond. If it clears, the mark publishes, and third parties get a window to object.

Only then does registration issue.

Knowing the shape of it is what stops the waiting from feeling like something has gone wrong.
items.cta: Save this so you know what to expect.

items.topic: What the examining attorney is actually looking for
items.hook: An examining attorney is not looking for reasons to say yes.
items.visual_concept: A precision measuring instrument abstracted into matte navy geometry, single key light
key_points: Whether the mark is likely to be confused with an existing registration
Whether the mark is merely descriptive or generic
Whether the specimen shows the mark used in commerce
Whether the description of goods and services is acceptable
items.caption_body:
The review is a check against specific grounds, not a general impression.

The examining attorney is asking whether your mark is likely to be confused with something already on the register. Whether it merely describes the goods rather than identifying their source. Whether the specimen shows the mark actually being used. Whether the description of goods and services is written in an acceptable form.

Each of those has a body of practice behind it.

Which is why applications rarely fail on the idea. They fail on one of four fairly predictable things — and three of them are decided before you file.

items.topic: What an Office Action is and what to do with one
items.hook: An Office Action is a question, not a verdict.
items.visual_concept: A sealed matte envelope form under a single hard key light, deep shadow behind
key_points: An Office Action raises an issue that needs a written response
Many are procedural and readily addressed
There is a response deadline and it is firm
No response generally means the application goes abandoned
items.caption_body:
The language is formal and it uses the word refusal, so people read it as a door closing. It is a request for a response.

Some Office Actions are procedural: tighten this description, add this disclaimer, replace this specimen. Others raise a substantive objection that needs a real argument.

Either way there is a deadline, and it is firm. Miss it and the application can go abandoned, which usually means starting over — including the filing fee.

The worst outcome here is not a difficult Office Action. It is an unopened one.
items.cta: Received an Office Action? DM us and we'll explain what it says.

items.topic: What publication and opposition mean for your mark
items.hook: Clearing examination is not the last hurdle. Publication is.
items.visual_concept: An open plaza rendered in cool architectural light, long shadows across a flat plane
key_points: An allowed mark is published so the public can see it
Third parties get a window to oppose registration
Most applications pass through without opposition
An opposition is a proceeding, not an automatic loss
items.caption_body:
Getting past the examining attorney feels like the finish line. There is one more step.

When a mark is allowed, it publishes — put in front of the public so that anyone who believes they would be harmed by the registration can say so.

Most applications go through this quietly. But an existing mark owner watching the register can file an opposition, and that starts a proceeding.

It is not an automatic loss, and it is not common. But it is the reason a mark is not truly settled the moment examination ends.
items.cta: Save this so you know what publication means.

items.topic: Filing before you have started selling
items.hook: You do not have to be selling yet to file. You do have to say so.
items.visual_concept: A form only partially materialised out of shadow, the remainder implied
key_points: There is a route for marks you have a genuine intention to use
It can secure an earlier priority date while you prepare to launch
Proof of actual use is still required before registration issues
Choosing the wrong basis creates problems later
items.caption_body:
A common blocker: the brand is ready, the product is not, and founders assume they have to wait.

There is a route for marks you genuinely intend to use. It lets you get in the queue and secure an earlier priority date while you finish building.

What it does not do is skip the use requirement. Before registration issues, you still have to show the mark actually working in commerce.

The important part is choosing the right basis at the start. Filing on the wrong one is one of those errors that is far easier to avoid than to correct.

items.topic: What you have to do after registration to keep it
items.hook: A registration is not permanent. It is renewable.
items.visual_concept: A cyclical form — a ring composed of repeating matte segments, one lit in teal
key_points: Registrations require maintenance filings at set intervals
Missing a maintenance deadline can cancel the registration
Continued use of the mark generally has to be shown
Diarising the dates is the whole job
items.caption_body:
People treat the registration certificate as the end of the process. It is the start of an obligation.

Registrations have to be maintained. At set intervals you file to confirm the mark is still in use, and if those windows pass unattended the registration can be cancelled — regardless of how well the brand is doing.

It is not difficult work. It is work that is easy to forget three, five, nine years after the last time you thought about it.

Put the dates in a calendar the day the certificate arrives. That is genuinely most of it.
items.cta: Save this the day your certificate arrives.

items.topic: How to track your application yourself
items.hook: You can check your application's status yourself, any time.
items.visual_concept: A single illuminated indicator on an otherwise dark instrument panel, matte finish
key_points: Your filing receipt carries a serial number
Public USPTO systems let you look up status with it
Status changes are visible without contacting anyone
Knowing where it sits removes most of the anxiety of waiting
items.caption_body:
Waiting is the hardest part of the process, mostly because it feels like nothing is happening.

Your filing receipt carries a serial number. The USPTO runs public systems where that number shows you exactly where the application sits — assigned, under examination, published, registered — and every document filed along the way.

You do not need permission and you do not need to ask anyone. It is public.

Check it monthly. It turns an unnerving silence into a visible queue position.
items.cta: Save this so you can track your own filing.

items.topic: The most common grounds for refusal
items.hook: Most refusals come down to a short list of predictable reasons.
items.visual_concept: A row of matte barriers at varying depths, one nearer and sharply lit
key_points: Likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark
The mark being merely descriptive of the goods or services
A specimen that fails to show use in commerce
Problems with the identification of goods and services
items.caption_body:
Applications do not usually fail for exotic reasons. They fail for a handful of recurring ones.

A mark too close to something already registered for related goods. A mark that describes the product instead of identifying its source. A specimen that shows a mockup rather than real use. A description of goods and services that is unacceptable as written.

That is the bulk of it.

Which is oddly encouraging, because three of those four are decided before you file — at the search, at the naming, and at the drafting. The process rewards the work done up front.
